relationship: Narrative parallel: received strength followed by offense against God
rationale: Hosea charges that those whose arms God strengthened devised evil against Him. Chronicles says Uzziah was wonderfully helped until he grew strong, then became proud and acted unjustly against the Lord; the earlier account names the Lord as the giver of his prosperity. Both contrast received strengthening with subsequent offense against its divine giver. Uzziah's specific sanctuary act is not assigned to Hosea's people, and Hosea's arms are not replaced by a particular military invention.

relationship: Rhetorical parallel: challenging alternative helpers in destruction
rationale: Hosea asks who will help Israel in destruction, between declaring that no one saves apart from God and challenging the king to save them. Deuteronomy similarly challenges trusted gods to arise and help, then declares that no god is beside the Lord and no one can deliver from His hands. Both questions expose the insufficiency of rival sources of rescue when God judges. Hosea's immediately challenged king is not equated with Deuteronomy's foreign gods.
